claims.text: A W-Ta-Cr-V high-entropy alloy can be prepared by magnetron sputtering.
Magnetron sputtering of the W-Ta-Cr-V alloy yields a uniform single-phase microstructure.
Inherent chemical disorder in high-entropy alloy catalysts produces local lattice distortions.
Chemical disorder and lattice distortions create a distribution of catalytically active sites with optimized adsorption energies.
The resulting adsorption-energy distribution enhances catalytic activity, selectivity, and durability relative to more homogeneous catalysts.
A mild thermal treatment will induce slight elemental segregation in the high-entropy alloy.
The mild thermal treatment will accentuate local lattice distortions without causing phase separation or significant grain growth.
Elemental segregation at grain boundaries and local lattice distortions modify the electronic structure and adsorption-energy landscape of the catalyst surface.
The modified electronic structure creates a broader distribution of surface binding strengths.
A balance of surface binding strengths promotes adsorption of reactive species and desorption of products.
Improved adsorption and desorption increase reaction rate.
The treated catalyst will have greater target-product selectivity than the untreated catalyst.
The treated catalyst will deactivate more slowly than the untreated catalyst.
The altered active-site distribution improves resistance to poisoning or sintering.
The hypothesis applies at 500–800 K when adsorption energetics govern the reaction and severe sintering or other uncontrolled microstructural changes do not occur.
An untreated high-entropy alloy baseline has minimal local lattice distortion and elemental segregation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes chemical disorder and local lattice distortion as inherent features of high-entropy alloys, whereas the proposed untreated high-entropy-alloy baseline is described as having minimal local lattice distortion and segregation.

The predicted causal effect requires performance improvement after the targeted structural modification, but the falsification rule requires both absent performance improvement and failure to confirm the structural modification. Thus, confirmed modification with no performance benefit would not formally falsify the hypothesis under the stated rule.
